{"id": "20:115/q17", "question": "How does Adam's story connect with the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Which nearby warning, narrative promise, preceding prophetic story, or broader sura theme supplies the link.", "positions": [{"id": "20:115/q17/p1", "position": "Adam's breach exemplifies the recurring neglect of Qur'anic warnings by later people.", "reasons": "Tabari and Tha'labi compare Adam with those disregarding the warnings of 20:113. Razi stresses that even direct warning about Satan did not avert error. Alusi defends this parallel against Ibn Atiyya; Asad and Razi take Adam as humanity's representative. Biqai extends the motif from Moses through the Reminder and repentance."}, {"id": "20:115/q17/p2", "position": "It warns Muhammad against haste and inadequate care in receiving revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Alusi link it to 20:114. Tabrisi says to trust God to preserve the Qur'an. Razi contrasts the Prophet's zealous excess with Adam's neglect, and says the need to ask for knowledge and protection from forgetting follows; his final variant reassures the Prophet that his haste came from devotion. Islahi compares Moses' haste and cites human hastiness in 21:37 and 17:11, urging gradual community training."}, {"id": "20:115/q17/p3", "position": "It fulfills the earlier promise to tell accounts of the past.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim and Razi point to 20:99; Biqai also mentions the Arabic judgment at 13:37. Alusi calls Abu Muslim's distant link weak."}, {"id": "20:115/q17/p4", "position": "It may open as a fresh, independently placed story.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya offers the option; Ibn Ashur's Aaron construction also makes the Adam account begin separately. Alusi dismisses the independent-beginning option as narrow."}, {"id": "20:115/q17/p5", "position": "It parallels Moses, Aaron, Israel, and the Samaritan in covenants, Satanic prompting, and forgetting.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares Israel's breach in 20:86, the Samaritan's prompted act in 20:96 with Satan's whisper in 20:120, and failure to remember in 20:16; he considers Moses' commission or Aaron's trust as a link. Islahi sees haste as the shared danger."}, {"id": "20:115/q17/p6", "position": "It illustrates God's mercy, forgiveness and forbearance after a lapse.", "reasons": "Qushayri says descendants should not despair. Biqai says God pardoned Adam without removing his chosen rank; Tabatabai links repentance with the promise of forgiveness in 20:82."}, {"id": "20:115/q17/p7", "position": "It shows an enduring human tendency to disobey or forget.", "reasons": "Baydawi invokes 46:27; Abu Hayyan says the retelling warns descendants about Satan's snares and follows the request for knowledge."}, {"id": "20:115/q17/p8", "position": "The placement after Surat Maryam connects Adam's account with correction of beliefs about Jesus.", "reasons": "KURANYOLU says Maryam treats Jesus' birth and mistaken beliefs, preparing its discussion of Adam and inherited sin."}]}
{"id": "20:115/q18", "question": "How does this telling of Adam relate to other Qur'anic tellings?", "turns_on": "The sources compare repetition, differences of emphasis, and the role of later guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:115/q18/p1", "position": "This is another retelling of Adam's temptation and expulsion, shaped by this passage's context.", "reasons": "Razi calls it the sixth telling after al-Baqara, al-A'raf, al-Hijr, al-Isra' and al-Kahf. KURANYOLU mentions Sad and al-A'raf, and the conditional Garden stay, temptation and expulsion; repeated accounts vary in style and context."}, {"id": "20:115/q18/p2", "position": "Unlike earlier tellings, this passage explicitly presents Adam's accepted repentance and chosen prophetic rank.", "reasons": "Attributed to Shawkani."}, {"id": "20:115/q18/p3", "position": "The close of the story makes Adam's forgetting a pattern for descendants who forget later guidance.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites 20:124; the tree ban prefigures divine guidance, though Adam lived before religious law."}]}
{"id": "20:115/q19", "question": "What does the Adam episode teach about human nature and divine response?", "turns_on": "The sources draw lessons about weakness, repentance, freedom from inherited guilt, and subsequent guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:115/q19/p1", "position": "Human beings are prone to Satanic temptation, heedlessness, haste and attachment to worldly pleasure.", "reasons": "Tabatabai depicts a well-provisioned Garden and warns that imagining worldly means confer mastery and lasting pleasure leads to suffering. Islahi says natural emotion and haste need patience; Biqai pairs human deficiency with divine forbearance and prompt repentance. Bursevi's hadith says even Adam's superior intellect could be affected by Satan. Study Quran calls Adam a model for humanity, citing God's teaching him all the names in 2:31."}, {"id": "20:115/q19/p2", "position": "God forgives a repentant person; Adam's lapse does not mean inherited original sin.", "reasons": "KURANYOLU says each person is tested with capacities usable for good or evil and can seek forgiveness directly; it rejects inherited guilt and Jesus' sacrificial cleansing. Biqai says Adam's high rank made his lapse count as sin under the maxim that a righteous person's good deed can be a fault for one brought near."}, {"id": "20:115/q19/p3", "position": "The Garden story explains religious guidance and the consequences of following or turning from it.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the compact twelve-verse account chiefly explains the institution of religion, reward for guidance, and punishment for turning away; the original Garden prohibition was advisory and prelegal."}]}
{"id": "20:115/q20", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from Adam's lapse?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is inward attention to God, self-regard, appetite, or dependence on grace.", "positions": [{"id": "20:115/q20/p1", "position": "True bliss is closeness to God; delight in the Garden or pride in one's action veils the giver.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata sets inward attention against sight of the Garden and against self-regard; Ja'far contrasts God with food and drink. Al-Wasiti makes self-restraint and witnessing servitude central. Ta'wilat Najmiyya describes desire darkening gnosis, and divine manifestation eclipsing Adam's created qualities."}, {"id": "20:115/q20/p2", "position": "Without God's grace, Satan's snare overcomes even Adam.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes Hafez's couplet."}]}
{"id": "20:115/q21", "question": "What is said about readings or textual variants cited near this verse?", "turns_on": "These notes address distinct textual or recitation observations; the NASHR items have no stated connection to this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "20:115/q21/p1", "position": "A report inserts the names of Muhammad, Ali, Fatima, Hasan, Husayn and the Imams into the verse.", "reasons": "Tabatabai calls al-Baqir's attributed insertion a report of textual distortion."}, {"id": "20:115/q21/p2", "position": "Ibn al-Jazari discusses unrelated hamza and plural-mim transmission precedents.", "reasons": "Makki permits separation of two hamzas for Ibn Dhakwan in أأعجمي and أأن كان by analogy to Hisham; Ibn al-Jazari cites an explicit al-Hashimi report from al-Shahrazuri and Ibn Khayrun linking plural mim before hamzat al-qat'. The notes give no link to the words of 20:115."}]}
{"id": "20:115/q22", "question": "What broader principle of Qur'anic coherence is recorded alongside this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether successive passages share a real unifying relation despite varied occasions of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:115/q22/p1", "position": "Coherence is a meaningful relation among verses and suras and can disclose subtleties of their ordering.", "reasons": "Burhan defines munasaba as nearness or likeness through rational, sensory, imaginative, causal, contrasting or external links, binding discourse like a building. Ibn al-Arabi treats connected verses as a great science; Razi locates many subtleties in arrangement. Itqan lists works by Ibn al-Zubayr, Biqai and Suyuti; Abu Bakr al-Nisaburi made the field prominent. Al-Malawi rejects dismissing coherence because revelation had separate circumstances."}, {"id": "20:115/q22/p2", "position": "Coherence should be sought where subject matter is unified; links across separate occasions and rulings can be contrived.", "reasons": "Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam argues from revelation across more than twenty years."}]}
{"id": "20:115/q23", "question": "What unrelated Ibn Abbas report appears in the collected notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:115/q23/p1", "position": "Migrants uncertain of their ancestry sought revelation and received the warning against distressing questions in 5:101.", "reasons": "The note says the account continues in the next segment and states no connection to 20:115."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q01", "question": "Why does God warn Adam at this point in the story?", "turns_on": "Whether the note explains the immediate narrative sequence or the lesson of its retelling.", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q01/p1", "position": "The warning follows Iblis's refusal to bow and counsels Adam for his protection.", "reasons": "Bursevi says God addressed Adam immediately after the refusal; Alusi says it was solicitous counsel; Tabataba'i says it followed the refusal and benefited Adam. {"id": "20:117/q02", "question": "Who is the enemy pointed out to Adam?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q02/p1", "position": "It is Iblis or Satan, whom Adam had just seen refuse to bow.", "reasons": "Tabari and Nasafi cite his refusal to prostrate and disobedience; Bursevi says the demonstrative points to the figure whose act Adam witnessed. Jishumi says his deception and whispering threaten the couple; Tabataba'i places the identification immediately after the refusal."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q03", "question": "Why is Iblis Adam's enemy?", "turns_on": "The sources offer envy, ignorance, opposed origins, refusal, and Satan's banishment as explanations; Tabataba'i rejects the motives he attributes to Razi.", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q03/p1", "position": "He resented Adam's favor and honor and envied him and his wife.", "reasons": "Razi, Bursevi and Alusi attribute the hostility to envy. Ibn Ashur says Satan thought himself more deserving of honor and envied the couple's knowledge of names, which enables thought, guidance and instruction (2:31). Islahi connects jealous refusal with Satan's challenge that humans deserved neither superiority nor Paradise, his respite and warning of Hell (7:14-22). Bursevi draws the general lesson that an envier works to ruin another's circumstances."}, {"id": "20:117/q03/p2", "position": "Iblis was an ignorant elder hostile to a young scholar, Adam.", "reasons": "Razi invokes Adam's knowledge of names (2:31) and Iblis's ignorant claim of superiority by ancestry. Bursevi adds a Persian couplet contrasting sight of Adam's body with sight of the divine light entrusted to him, and the maxim that one is an enemy of what one does not know; Alusi repeats the ignorant-versus-learned explanation."}, {"id": "20:117/q03/p3", "position": "Their opposing origins produced inherited hostility: Iblis from fire and Adam from earth and water.", "reasons": "Razi and Bursevi contrast fire with Adam's water and earth; Alusi says Adam was made from clay and Hawwa from Adam."}, {"id": "20:117/q03/p4", "position": "His expulsion from divine proximity and curse after humanity's precedence caused his hostility.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i appeals to Satan's own speech (15:39): honor and prostration concerned humankind as a species, whose precedence led to Satan's banishment and curse (17:62). He dismisses Razi's proposed motives as specious."}, {"id": "20:117/q03/p5", "position": "His refusal to prostrate showed that he did not accept Adam.", "reasons": "Tabari cites the refusal and disobedience (2:34); Nasafi says he did not accept Adam."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q04", "question": "What does the demonstrative 'this' contribute?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q04/p1", "position": "Pointing to Satan conveys contempt and makes the witnessed figure vivid.", "reasons": "Bursevi says Adam had just witnessed Satan's deed. Ibn Ashur compares the contemptuous demonstrative with the pagans' dismissive reference to the man criticizing their gods (21:36), and contrasts this verse with al-A'raf 7:22, which names Satan directly."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q05", "question": "Who is Adam's 'zawj,' and what does that word denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q05/p1", "position": "Adam's zawj is Eve; the term denotes either member of a pair accompanied by another of its kind.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Bursevi name Eve or Hawwa. Bursevi defines zawj for either sex. Bint al-Shati notes the Quran's use of zawj for Adam's spouse in 2:35, 7:19 and 20:117."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q06", "question": "Why is the preposition repeated in 'to you and to your wife'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q06/p1", "position": "The repeated lam is required to coordinate with a genitive pronoun and can also emphasize that Eve is independently Satan's enemy.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes the grammatical requirement to most grammarians and says obligation can coexist with Ibn Malik's contextual emphasis. Some whom he cites stress that enmity toward Eve is intrinsic, not merely derived from enmity toward Adam. Burhan reports both a strengthening lam and attachment to an implied predicate specifying the enemy as yours."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q07", "question": "Why call Eve 'your wife' rather than naming her?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q07/p1", "position": "The relational name strengthens Adam's aversion to Satan and the warning.", "reasons": "Alusi says calling her Adam's wife rather than Hawwa intensifies the warning. Ibn Ashur says this verse, unlike al-A'raf's general statement (7:22), identifies Adam as the original target and Eve as the extension through her relation to him."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q08", "question": "What does the warning against Satan expelling the couple require, and why is expulsion assigned to him?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q08/p1", "position": "Adam and Eve must not heed Satan or put themselves within his power; his temptation causes the act leading to expulsion, though God effects it.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Atiyya say obedience to Satan brings disobedience and expulsion. Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Study Quran identify accepting his temptation, the latter naming the forbidden tree. Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Tabataba'i and Alusi explain the prohibition indirectly as preventing Satan from becoming the cause; Tabataba'i adds vigilance against his scheme. Razi, Bursevi and Abu Hayyan distinguish Satan as cause from God as actual expeller. Samin says the surface prohibition addresses Iblis but intends Adam and Eve; Biqa'i says that form spares her direct prohibition and intensifies warning; Ibn Ashur says it pointedly forbids Adam being swayed, not merely letting news of his deed reach God. Alusi compares 7:2. Yahya says their disobedience would lead God to expel them."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q09", "question": "How does the fa connect the warning to the enemy statement?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q09/p1", "position": "It makes the prohibition follow from Satan's enmity or from God's disclosure of that enmity.", "reasons": "Alusi gives both possible antecedents; Ibn Ashur says an enemy seeks his opponent's harm, hence the need to beware."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q10", "question": "What hardship does 'you will suffer' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether shaqa names all earthly distress or especially earning sustenance; Alusi favors the broader scope, while others cite labor and the following verses.", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q10/p1", "position": "It is the broad toil and distress of earthly life after the Garden, including the effort needed for food, clothing, drink and shelter.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas via Wahidi calls it worldly toil and distress; al-Hasan says all descendants labor and no one escapes toil. Qushayri says both spouses face hardship. Alusi explicitly prefers this breadth over restriction to earning, despite support in 20:118-119. Tabataba'i says the following verses explain the necessities. Biqa'i says it is worldly, not ultimate misery, since Adam later entered the Garden and the consequence after fa cannot fail. Raghib, cited by Bursevi, distinguishes worldly and afterlife hardship and personal, bodily and external forms; al-Qamus gives shaqa as hardship and difficulty with a long final vowel. Asad renders it becoming unhappy and points to his note on the Garden."}, {"id": "20:117/q10/p2", "position": "It is specifically the labor of earning food or a livelihood by one's own hands and sweat.", "reasons": "Muqatil contrasts effortless eating in the Garden with work afterward. Yahya reports work by hand and sweat of brow; Tabari, Thalabi, Baghawi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and Study Quran speak of earning by labor. Wahidi transmits Zayd ibn Ali's gloss; al-Farra via Qurtubi says eating from one's own work. Suddi specifies plowing, planting, kneading and baking; Baghawi's version adds harvesting and grinding. Baydawi cites 20:118-119 for the male livelihood reading. Study Quran cites 2:36 and 7:24-25 for life on earth."}, {"id": "20:117/q10/p3", "position": "It is bodily hardship assigned to Adam specifically, distinct from the shared expulsion.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this view and says the following account of Garden life clarifies bodily hardship."}, {"id": "20:117/q10/p4", "position": "It can be called unhappiness or wretchedness, contrasted with happiness.", "reasons": "Asad gives the literal sense 'so that thou wilt become unhappy' and refers to his Garden note; Raghib, quoted by Bursevi, contrasts hardship with happiness across worldly and afterlife categories."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q11", "question": "What reports illustrate Adam's labor after descent?", "turns_on": "The accounts differ on the ox's color and Adam's blaming Eve, and one account uses grain and a loaf instead.", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q11/p1", "position": "A red ox or bull was sent to Adam; he plowed with it and wiped sweat from his brow.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr is named by Thalabi, Wahidi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Qurtubi; Tabari names Sa'id. Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Razi and Nasafi give the account without naming him. Abu Hayyan's Ibn Jubayr version says Adam ate by his hand's labor. Details vary between being given the animal and descending with it."}, {"id": "20:117/q11/p2", "position": "Adam worked an ox, recognized the warned toil, and blamed Eve; the blame recurred among descendants.", "reasons": "Sufyan's transmission from Sa'id ibn Jubayr in Durr mentions Adam's recognition, his blame of Eve, and descendants repeating that blame when working oxen; no color is supplied."}, {"id": "20:117/q11/p3", "position": "Adam worked a piebald ox, recognized the toil, and blamed Hawwa.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes this to Sa'id ibn Jubayr and names Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Asakir and others as transmitters; he states no grading. The color is piebald rather than the red of other reports."}, {"id": "

{"id": "20:117/q12", "question": "Why is 'you will suffer' singular after the dual warning?", "turns_on": "Explanations appeal to Adam's role in the household, his status as addressee, shared consequences, verse cadence, courtesy, or bodily toil; Tabataba'i rejects the provider and cadence proposals.", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q12/p1", "position": "Adam bears or represents the household's labor as its head and provider, so his hardship includes his wife's.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Qushayri, Jishumi, Baghawi, Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi's Mawardi report, Qurtubi, Biqa'i and others connect the form to the man's work or maintenance. Kashshaf, Razi and Baydawi say a household head's hardship and happiness encompass the family. Abu Hayyan says household hardship follows Adam's; Ibn Ashur adds concision and says one spouse's suffering affects the other. Thalabi and Baghawi stress that Adam's toil was greater. Bursevi says it principally fell on him; Alusi says he is primary in household affairs. Tabataba'i rejects the provider explanation because the following verses also address Adam singularly, which that explanation would require to be dual."}, {"id": "20:117/q12/p2", "position": "Adam is the initial, principal or direct addressee; naming his consequence suffices within an Arabic singular-for-dual construction.", "reasons": "Tabari and al-Farra compare the singular sitter of the two recording angels in 50:17. Ibn Qutayba and Burhan compare Pharaoh's address to Moses and Aaron naming Moses alone. Ibn Atiyya, cited also in Burhan and Itqan, calls Adam the first addressee and main subject. Tabataba'i says the covenant and speech were directed to Adam and the account shifts to dual only where both must be included. Ibn Ata instead says Adam knew the special rank of direct address and Eve followed him. Itqan observes Arabic singular for dual."}, {"id": "20:117/q12/p3", "position": "The singular preserves the surrounding verse endings and cadence.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Qushayri, al-Farra via Wahidi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Tabrisi, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Samin, Bursevi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur give this explanation, often alongside household reasons. Tabataba'i dismisses it."}, {"id": "20:117/q12/p4", "position": "Both spouses share the cause and effects, so the singular includes Eve and can extend to descendants.", "reasons": "Mawardi says the cause applies equally to both; Qushayri says God knew both would suffer. Jishumi and Tabrisi give the shared cause. Qurtubi says the singular intends the wife too. Sufyan says Eve entered with Adam and compares singular addresses to the Prophet including others in 65:1 and 66:1, extending the meaning to descendants. Ibn Ashur says one spouse's suffering affects the other."}, {"id": "20:117/q12/p5", "position": "The woman is courteously left unnamed in the singular consequence.", "reasons": "Burhan and Itqan report polite omission, the latter citing a saying that good manners conceal women."}, {"id": "20:117/q12/p6", "position": "Only Adam is assigned bodily hardship, though both are expelled.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports that the following Garden descriptions clarify this distinction."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q13", "question": "What is the grammatical mood and force of 'fa-tashqa'?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is the syntactic consequence of the prohibition or a fresh indicative prediction; Samin and Alusi reject the latter force.", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q13/p1", "position": "It is subjunctive after an implied an in response to the prohibition, expressing its consequence.", "reasons": "Samin explicitly supplies the implied an. Abu Hayyan and Alusi allow this analysis; Alusi favors consequence and rejects mere prediction. Biqa'i says the predicate after fa cannot fail, so ultimate misery cannot be intended."}, {"id": "20:117/q13/p2", "position": "It is indicative in a new sentence: 'then you will suffer.'", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan allows a separate prediction. Samin reports the Shaykh's proposal but considers it remote or impossible because the point is more than prediction; Alusi likewise rejects the predictive force."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q14", "question": "What does the warning imply about the consequence of disobedience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q14/p1", "position": "The prohibition is advisory; disobedience brings natural earthly toil, not an afterlife penalty for a legislated sin.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i says the warning preceded religious legislation and explains the result as labor for human needs. Biqa'i argues that the threatened misery cannot be ultimate misery since Adam later entered the Garden and the consequence after fa is certain."}, {"id": "20:117/q14/p2", "position": "Even a warned believer may fail to recall the enemy and later regret a settled decree.", "reasons": "Qushayri says Adam's faith, warning and certainty were unsurpassed, yet he failed to recall the enemy during the whispering, then regretted and wept when hardship came. Bursevi says awareness of the kinds of misery makes one recoil, while caution cannot defeat destiny."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q15", "question": "What duty toward a wife is drawn from Adam's singular toil?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q15/p1", "position": "A husband owes his wife maintenance, covering food, drink, clothing and housing.", "reasons": "Qurtubi derives the duty from Adam bearing the toil and lists the four necessities. Tabrisi and Biqa'i connect Adam's work to support and care for his wife; Biqa'i adds that an upright husband guides her to good while a corrupt one leads her to harm."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q16", "question": "How do the next verses explain this threatened hardship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q16/p1", "position": "Garden freedom from hunger, nakedness, thirst and sun exposure displays the food, clothing, drink and shelter that expulsion would cost.", "reasons": "Razi identifies these four protections as the explanation of misery. Biqa'i names satiety, drink, clothing and shelter as supports of sufficiency and says their negated opposites make Adam recoil from the cause while learning destiny's force. Tabataba'i and Baydawi cite 20:118-119 as support for the needs and effort involved; Qurtubi names the four maintenance necessities."}, {"id": "20:117/q16/p2", "position": "The worldly hardship here leads into the later mention of hardship for one who rejects guidance.", "reasons": "Raghib, cited by Bursevi, connects the worldly sense here with the afterlife hardship mentioned in 20:123."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q17", "question": "What practical lesson do the sources draw from warning about an enemy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q17/p1", "position": "Listening to an enemy brings regret after it can no longer help.", "reasons": "Qushayri draws this lesson and cites Adam's later regret and weeping despite unsurpassed faith and certainty; he says Adam did not recall the divine identification when Satan whispered. Bursevi generalizes that envy turns a person into an enemy bent on ruining another."}, {"id": "20:117/q17/p2", "position": "Adam concealed his enemy's hostility and failed to ask God for protection, so he listened to the enemy's speech and oath.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti is reported by Sulami; his explanation ties the lapse to reliance on what the enemy said and swore."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q18", "question": "How is this account connected with the other Quranic accounts of Adam and Satan?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q18/p1", "position": "It retells the warning, temptation and fall already narrated elsewhere, adapting the details and style to this sura.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu compares earlier accounts in Sad and al-A'raf, including the conditional Garden stay, enticement and expulsion, citing 2:30 and 7:11. Study Quran points to 7:21-22 for the warning and 2:35-37 and 7:19-23 for deception, fall and remorse. Ibn Ashur says al-Baqara and al-A'raf already told creation and prostration and notes this verse's demonstrative versus naming Satan in 7:22; he also notes the fuller identification of Adam and Eve as targets here. Islahi draws on 7:14-22 for Satan's challenge, respite and the warning."}]}
{"id": "20:117/q19", "question": "What does the adjacent mention of Iblis's refusal mean lexically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:117/q19/p1", "position": "Iblis may derive from bewildered despair or be foreign; iba' is an especially strong refusal.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes al-Qamus for both etymologies of Iblis, and al-Mufradat for the distinction that every iba' is refusal but not every refusal is iba'. {"id": "20:118/q08", "question": "How are hunger, nakedness, thirst, and sun exposure paired and ordered?", "turns_on": "Whether the order follows shared inner and outer effects, separates expected counterparts for emphasis, ranks needs by importance, or serves a wrap-and-unfold rhyme pattern; al-Ālūsī disputes two poetic or rhyme arguments.", "positions": [{"id": "20:118/q08/p1", "position": "The pairs link inner and outer afflictions: hunger with nakedness, then thirst with the sun's heat.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī calls hunger and nakedness inner and outer deprivation, while heat causes thirst.
